decisions.title: Fixed Protocol Message Envelope
decisions.description: Protocol messages carry a fixed envelope: type, from, to, request_id, and payload. This structure travels together so one workflow can always be parsed and handled the same way. The request_id enables correlation: when a response comes back, it references the same request_id, so the sender knows which request was answered.
decisions.alternatives: Free-form messages in a mailbox are simpler but make correlation unreliable. A type system with inheritance is more flexible but loses the predictability of a fixed envelope.

decisions.title: Request Records Persisted to Disk
decisions.description: Protocol requests create durable RequestRecord files with state transitions: pending, approved, rejected, expired. These records survive context compression and process restarts. Approval, shutdown, or handoff should be inspectable after the fact. The record is the source of truth for protocol state, not any agent's memory.
decisions.alternatives: In-memory request tracking is simpler but loses state on crash. Tracking requests only in messages[] means they are lost during context compression. Durable records provide the persistence that multi-turn coordination requires.

decisions.title: State Machine Transitions Are the Teaching Spine
decisions.description: The pending -> approved -> executed -> completed lifecycle is the real content of the protocols chapter. The human-readable message text is only the explanation layer around that state machine. Teaching protocols as 'more formal chat' misses the point: the important part is the request correlation and state transitions that make coordination reliable.
decisions.alternatives: Teaching protocols as message formatting exercises loses the state machine insight. Treating them as API contracts is correct but overly abstract for the teaching context.
